title: Create S3 buckets
content:
contract-risk-docs-* holds contract files and results in the quarantine/, clean/, results/<job_id>/ layout. contract-risk-legal-* holds original legal documents under the legal/ prefix. Both block public access, use SSE-S3 encryption (the default) and reject any request that does not use HTTPS.
Create both buckets: source ~/cr.env echo "export DOCS_BUCKET=contract-risk-docs-$ACCOUNT_ID LEGAL_BUCKET=contract-risk-legal-$ACCOUNT_ID" >> ~/cr.env source ~/cr.env for B in "$DOCS_BUCKET" "$LEGAL_BUCKET"; do aws s3api create-bucket --bucket "$B" --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint="$AWS_REGION" aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket "$B" --public-access-block-configuration \ BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true cat > /tmp/tls-only.json <<EOF {"Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{"Sid": "DenyInsecureTransport", "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:*", "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::$B", "arn:aws:s3:::$B/*"], "Condition": {"Bool": {"aws:SecureTransport": "false"}}}]} EOF aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket "$B" --policy file:///tmp/tls-only.json done 📸 Screenshot to take: S3 console → Buckets: the contract-risk-docs-... and contract-risk-legal-... buckets in Asia Pacific (Singapore).
📸 Screenshot to take: Open the contract-risk-docs-... bucket → Permissions tab: Block all public access = On and the DenyInsecureTransport bucket policy.
(Cost optimisation, optional) Expire files left in quarantine/ after 7 days: cat > /tmp/lifecycle.json <<'EOF' {"Rules": [{"ID": "expire-quarantine", "Status": "Enabled", "Filter": {"Prefix": "quarantine/"}, "Expiration": {"Days": 7}}]} EOF aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket "$DOCS_BUCKET" --lifecycle-configuration file:///tmp/lifecycle.json

title: Create the VPC, subnet and Security Group
content:
Run these in CloudShell.
Create the 10.0.0.0/16 VPC and enable DNS hostnames (needed by Session Manager and endpoints): source ~/cr.env VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 \ --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=vpc,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=contract-risk-vpc}]' \ --query Vpc.VpcId --output text) aws ec2 modify-vpc-attribute --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" --enable-dns-hostnames '{"Value":true}' echo "export VPC_ID=$VPC_ID" >> ~/cr.env Create the 10.0.1.0/24 subnet in ap-southeast-1a with auto-assigned public IPv4, so EC2 reaches the Internet without a NAT Gateway: SUBNET_ID=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 \ --availability-zone ap-southeast-1a \ --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=contract-risk-subnet-a}]' \ --query Subnet.SubnetId --output text) aws ec2 modify-subnet-attribute --subnet-id "$SUBNET_ID" --map-public-ip-on-launch echo "export SUBNET_ID=$SUBNET_ID" >> ~/cr.env Create the Internet Gateway, the route table and the default route: IGW_ID=$(aws ec2 create-internet-gateway \ --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=internet-gateway,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=contract-risk-igw}]' \ --query InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId --output text) aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --internet-gateway-id "$IGW_ID" --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" RT_ID=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" \ --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=route-table,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=contract-risk-rt}]' \ --query RouteTable.RouteTableId --output text) aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id "$RT_ID" --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id "$IGW_ID" aws ec2 associate-route-table --route-table-id "$RT_ID" --subnet-id "$SUBNET_ID" echo "export IGW_ID=$IGW_ID RT_ID=$RT_ID" >> ~/cr.env 📸 Screenshot to take: VPC console → Your VPCs → select contract-risk-vpc → Resource map tab: subnet, route table contract-risk-rt and the Internet Gateway visible.
Create the Security Group: remove the default allow-all outbound rule and only allow TCP 443 out (AWS APIs, Gemini, Qdrant, Supabase, Tavily, Langfuse, GitHub, Docker Hub) and TCP 80 (Ubuntu apt mirrors). Add no inbound rule. SG_ID=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name contract-risk-ec2-sg \ --description "ContractGuard AI EC2: no inbound, outbound 80/443 only" --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" \ --query GroupId --output text) aws ec2 revoke-security-group-egress --group-id "$SG_ID" \ --ip-permissions '[{"IpProtocol":"-1","IpRanges":[{"CidrIp":"0.0.0.0/0"}]}]' aws ec2 authorize-security-group-egress --group-id "$SG_ID" --ip-permissions \ '[{"IpProtocol":"tcp","FromPort":443,"ToPort":443,"IpRanges":[{"CidrIp":"0.0.0.0/0"}]}, {"IpProtocol":"tcp","FromPort":80,"ToPort":80,"IpRanges":[{"CidrIp":"0.0.0.0/0"}]}]' echo "export SG_ID=$SG_ID" >> ~/cr.env The 9 containers talk to each other over the backend Docker network inside the host, so no port needs opening. The monitoring service only binds 127.0.0.1:8099 for the data pipeline on the same host.
📸 Screenshot to take: EC2 console → Security Groups → contract-risk-ec2-sg: the Inbound rules tab is empty, the Outbound rules tab only has TCP 80 and 443.

title: Introduction
content:
The problem ContractGuard users upload contracts to the web app. The AI side (this repository) receives jobs through SQS, reads the file from S3, has three agents classify clauses, score risk against Vietnamese law and propose rewrites, then returns the result through S3/SQS. The web app never calls the model directly: everything goes through queues and S3 objects.
Architecture and data flow 📸 Screenshot to take: Your own architecture diagram drawn in draw.io with the AWS Architecture Icons (you may reuse the Proposal image). Export a PNG and save it over static/images/5-Workshop/5.1-Workshop-overview/architecture.png.
# Step Components 1 Receive the job: long-poll analysis-requests, read results/<job_id>/request.json and the file in quarantine/ SQS, S3, worker 2 Hold the job lease and record progress DynamoDB contract-risk-jobs, contract-risk-job-events 3 Text extraction, OCR, chunking with source positions input-processing 4 Orchestration: Agent 1 per chunk → aggregate → Agent 2 → Agent 3 langgraph, agent-1/2/3 5 Model calls Google Gemini API 6 Legal lookup (hybrid RAG + rerank, web search) mcp → Qdrant, Supabase, Tavily, reference S3 7 Python scoring, schema check, write clean/ + extraction.json, send completed, delete the message langgraph, worker, S3, SQS 8 Fetch secrets at start-up config → Secrets Manager (IAM role) 9 Events from every service, trace export monitoring → Langfuse 10 Scheduled legal collection SQS data-update → collector → S3 + processor → Supabase, Qdrant Differences from the project’s real environment The real environment uses two AWS accounts: the contract queues and bucket belong to the ContractGuard web account, EC2 belongs to the AI account, and cross-account access uses resource policies. So that you can reproduce it, the workshop puts everything in one account and plays the web back end with the AWS CLI (writing request.json and sending messages yourself).
A subnet with an Internet Gateway and a Security Group with no inbound port instead of a private subnet + NAT Gateway: EC2 still accepts no connection from outside, without paying hourly NAT charges. Traffic to S3 and DynamoDB goes through VPC Gateway Endpoints (free). No SSH: EC2 is managed through AWS Systems Manager Session Manager; no key pair, no port 22.

title: Launch EC2
content:
Suggested configuration: Ubuntu 24.04, t3.xlarge (4 vCPU, 16 GiB RAM: the embedding and reranker models run on CPU and each process loads about 2.2 GB of model), an encrypted 60 GB gp3 volume (images + build cache + ~3.3 GB of models). Pick another instance type to match your cost estimate if needed.
HttpPutResponseHopLimit=2 is mandatory. With 1, the host gets credentials but Docker containers do not (NoCredentialsError), because IMDS requests from a container cross one more hop through the bridge network.
Launch the instance from CloudShell, with no key pair: source ~/cr.env AMI_ID=$(aws ssm get-parameter \ --name /aws/service/canonical/ubuntu/server/24.04/stable/current/amd64/hvm/ebs-gp3/ami-id \ --query Parameter.Value --output text) INSTANCE_ID=$(aws ec2 run-instances --image-id "$AMI_ID" --instance-type t3.xlarge \ --subnet-id "$SUBNET_ID" --security-group-ids "$SG_ID" \ --iam-instance-profile Name=ContractRisk-EC2-Profile \ --metadata-options HttpEndpoint=enabled,HttpTokens=required,HttpPutResponseHopLimit=2 \ --block-device-mappings '[{"DeviceName":"/dev/sda1","Ebs":{"VolumeSize":60,"VolumeType":"gp3","Encrypted":true}}]' \ --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=contract-risk-ec2}]' \ --query 'Instances[0].InstanceId' --output text) echo "export INSTANCE_ID=$INSTANCE_ID" >> ~/cr.env aws ec2 wait instance-status-ok --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" \ --query 'Reservations[0].Instances[0].[State.Name,MetadataOptions.HttpTokens,MetadataOptions.HttpPutResponseHopLimit]' 📸 Screenshot to take: EC2 console → Instances → contract-risk-ec2: Instance state = Running, Status check = 2/2, the Security tab showing IAM role ContractRisk-EC2-Role and Security Group contract-risk-ec2-sg.
📸 Screenshot to take: Select the instance → Actions → Instance settings → Modify instance metadata options: IMDSv2 = Required, Metadata response hop limit = 2 (take the screenshot, then Cancel).
Connect with Session Manager: EC2 console → select contract-risk-ec2 → Connect → Session Manager → Connect, then switch to the ubuntu user: sudo su - ubuntu 📸 Screenshot to take: EC2 console → select the instance → Connect → Session Manager tab → Connect: the browser terminal after running sudo su - ubuntu and whoami.

title: Test the analysis flow
content:
Upload sample-contract.pdf to CloudShell first (Actions → Upload file).
Ping/pong handshake to make sure the worker reads the queue and can publish results: source ~/cr.env PING_ID=$(python3 -c "import uuid; print(uuid.uuid4())") aws sqs send-message --queue-url "$REQ_URL" \ --message-body "{\"message_version\":\"1\",\"event_type\":\"ping\",\"job_id\":\"$PING_ID\"}" aws sqs receive-message --queue-url "$RES_URL" --wait-time-seconds 20 --max-number-of-messages 10 \ --query 'Messages[].Body' --output text 📸 Screenshot to take: CloudShell: the ping command and the receive-message output with an "event_type": "pong" message for the same job_id.
Submit an analysis job following the protocol: file in quarantine/, ticket results/<job_id>/request.json, analysis_requested message: source ~/cr.env JOB_ID=$(python3 -c "import uuid; print(uuid.uuid4())") CONTRACT_ID=$(python3 -c "import uuid; print(uuid.uuid4())") echo "export JOB_ID=$JOB_ID CONTRACT_ID=$CONTRACT_ID" >> ~/cr.env aws s3 cp sample-contract.pdf "s3://$DOCS_BUCKET/quarantine/lab-user/$JOB_ID.pdf" cat > request.json <<EOF { "schema_version": "1.0.0", "job_id": "$JOB_ID", "tenant_id": "lab-tenant", "contract_id": "$CONTRACT_ID", "contract_version": "1", "source_file_key": "quarantine/lab-user/$JOB_ID.pdf", "clean_file_key": "clean/lab-workspace/$CONTRACT_ID/v1/source.pdf", "result_key": "results/$JOB_ID/extraction.json", "declared_file_type": "pdf", "output_language": "vi", "context": {"own_party": "buyer", "contract_type": "service_agreement", "has_personal_data": true}, "limits": {"max_pages": 100, "max_bytes": 20971520} } EOF aws s3 cp request.json "s3://$DOCS_BUCKET/results/$JOB_ID/request.json" aws sqs send-message --queue-url "$REQ_URL" --message-body \ "{\"message_version\":\"1\",\"event_type\":\"analysis_requested\",\"job_id\":\"$JOB_ID\",\"request_key\":\"results/$JOB_ID/request.json\"}" date -u +"submitted at %H:%M:%S UTC" 📸 Screenshot to take: CloudShell after the job submission block: the upload: lines for the file and request.json, the SQS MessageId and the submission time.
Follow it on EC2 (Session Manager): cd /opt/contract-risk-management docker compose logs -f --tail 20 worker langgraph agent-1 agent-2 agent-3 📸 Screenshot to take: EC2 logs while the job runs: the worker taking the job, langgraph calling agent_1 per chunk, then agent_2, agent_3, and the completion line.
Check progress in DynamoDB (this is also how the web app reads the job’s progress bar): source ~/cr.env aws dynamodb get-item --table-name contract-risk-jobs \ --key "{\"job_id\":{\"S\":\"contract:$CONTRACT_ID\"}}" \ --projection-expression "active_job_id, stage, progress" --output json 📸 Screenshot to take: The get-item output: stage (e.g. agent_2_risk_scoring...) and increasing progress; take another one after the job finishes.
Check the result once the logs report completion: source ~/cr.env aws sqs receive-message --queue-url "$RES_URL" --wait-time-seconds 20 --max-number-of-messages 10 \ --query 'Messages[].Body' --output text aws s3 ls "s3://$DOCS_BUCKET/results/$JOB_ID/" aws s3 ls "s3://$DOCS_BUCKET/clean/lab-workspace/$CONTRACT_ID/v1/" aws s3 ls "s3://$DOCS_BUCKET/quarantine/lab-user/" | grep "$JOB_ID" || echo "quarantine copy removed" aws s3 cp "s3://$DOCS_BUCKET/results/$JOB_ID/extraction.json" . jq 'keys' extraction.json jq '{clauses: (.clauses | length), findings: (.findings | length), checks: (.checks | length), scoring: .scoring}' extraction.json 📸 Screenshot to take: The check block output: the progress and completed messages (with result_key), the extraction.json file, the clean/.../source.pdf copy, the removed quarantine/ copy, and the jq summary (clauses, findings, checks, scoring).
Pass criteria: a completed message carrying result_key; a valid extraction.json with clauses, findings, 20 checks and a scoring block; the clean/ copy exists; the quarantine/ copy is deleted; the analysis-requests message is deleted (queue back to 0). Record the processing time (submission to the completed message) for the report.

title: Create SQS queues with a Dead-Letter Queue
content:
Queue Sender → receiver Visibility timeout contract-risk-analysis-requests Web (you, via CLI) → worker 900 s: long jobs, the worker extends it contract-risk-analysis-results Worker → web (progress, completed, failed, pong, chat_answered) 60 s contract-risk-chat-requests Web → the worker’s chat process 300 s contract-risk-data-update Collection schedule → collector ({"mode":"incremental"}) 900 s A message received more than 3 times without being deleted moves to the DLQ, so one bad message cannot make the worker loop forever.
source ~/cr.env make_queue() { # $1 = queue name, $2 = visibility timeout (seconds) local dlq_url dlq_arn dlq_url=$(aws sqs create-queue --queue-name "$1-dlq" --attributes SqsManagedSseEnabled=true \ --query QueueUrl --output text) dlq_arn=$(aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url "$dlq_url" --attribute-names QueueArn \ --query Attributes.QueueArn --output text) cat > /tmp/attrs.json <<EOF {"VisibilityTimeout": "$2", "ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds": "20", "SqsManagedSseEnabled": "true", "RedrivePolicy": "{\"deadLetterTargetArn\":\"$dlq_arn\",\"maxReceiveCount\":\"3\"}"} EOF aws sqs create-queue --queue-name "$1" --attributes file:///tmp/attrs.json --query QueueUrl --output text } REQ_URL=$(make_queue contract-risk-analysis-requests 900) RES_URL=$(make_queue contract-risk-analysis-results 60) CHAT_URL=$(make_queue contract-risk-chat-requests 300) DATA_URL=$(make_queue contract-risk-data-update 900) echo "export REQ_URL=$REQ_URL RES_URL=$RES_URL CHAT_URL=$CHAT_URL DATA_URL=$DATA_URL" >> ~/cr.env aws sqs list-queues --queue-name-prefix contract-risk --output table 📸 Screenshot to take: SQS console → Queues, filtered by contract-risk: 4 main queues and 4 -dlq queues, Encryption = SSE-SQS.
📸 Screenshot to take: Open contract-risk-analysis-requests → Dead-letter queue tab: points to ...-dlq, Maximum receives = 3; Details tab: Visibility timeout = 15 minutes.

title: Create VPC Gateway Endpoints
content:
The worker reads and writes S3 and DynamoDB constantly. A Gateway Endpoint adds a route to the service prefix list in the route table, so traffic stays on the AWS network instead of the Internet Gateway, at no charge.
Create endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB attached to the subnet’s route table: source ~/cr.env for SVC in s3 dynamodb; do aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" --vpc-endpoint-type Gateway \ --service-name "com.amazonaws.$AWS_REGION.$SVC" --route-table-ids "$RT_ID" \ --tag-specifications "ResourceType=vpc-endpoint,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=contract-risk-$SVC-gwe}]" \ --query VpcEndpoint.VpcEndpointId --output text done Check their state: aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints --filters Name=vpc-id,Values="$VPC_ID" \ --query 'VpcEndpoints[].[ServiceName,VpcEndpointType,State]' --output table 📸 Screenshot to take: VPC console → Endpoints: the com.amazonaws.ap-southeast-1.s3 and ...dynamodb endpoints, type Gateway, status Available.
📸 Screenshot to take: VPC console → Route tables → contract-risk-rt → Routes tab: two pl-... destinations pointing to vpce-... next to the 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-... route.
SQS, Secrets Manager and the external APIs still go through the Internet Gateway (TLS). To move EC2 into a fully private subnet you would add Interface Endpoints for SQS, Secrets Manager and SSM plus a NAT Gateway for Gemini/Qdrant/Supabase; both are billed per hour (see the Cost estimation section).

title: Error scenarios and automated tests
content:
The system must reject bad input with a failed message carrying an error code instead of a stuck job. The submit helper below resends the valid ticket from step 5.7.1 with one field changed.
source ~/cr.env submit() { # $1 = scenario name, $2 = jq filter applied to the valid request.json local id; id=$(python3 -c "import uuid; print(uuid.uuid4())") aws s3 cp sample-contract.pdf "s3://$DOCS_BUCKET/quarantine/lab-user/$id.pdf" > /dev/null jq --arg id "$id" '.job_id=$id | .source_file_key="quarantine/lab-user/\($id).pdf" | .result_key="results/\($id)/extraction.json" | '"$2" request.json > "req-$1.json" aws s3 cp "req-$1.json" "s3://$DOCS_BUCKET/results/$id/request.json" > /dev/null aws sqs send-message --queue-url "$REQ_URL" --message-body \ "{\"message_version\":\"1\",\"event_type\":\"analysis_requested\",\"job_id\":\"$id\",\"request_key\":\"results/$id/request.json\"}" > /dev/null echo "$1 -> $id" } submit wrong-type '.declared_file_type="docx"' submit too-many-pages '.limits.max_pages=1' aws sqs send-message --queue-url "$REQ_URL" --message-body "not a json message" sleep 60 aws sqs receive-message --queue-url "$RES_URL" --wait-time-seconds 20 --max-number-of-messages 10 \ --query 'Messages[].Body' --output text 📸 Screenshot to take: CloudShell: the failed messages received, showing the error_code (e.g. ERR-AI-001, ERR-UPL-004) and failure_reason of each job.
After 3 receives without success the broken message moves to the DLQ (with a 900 s visibility timeout this takes about 45 minutes; check back later):
source ~/cr.env aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url "${REQ_URL}-dlq" \ --attribute-names ApproximateNumberOfMessages --output text 📸 Screenshot to take: SQS console → contract-risk-analysis-requests-dlq → Send and receive messages → Poll for messages: the not a json message message (or the ApproximateNumberOfMessages output).
Record what you observe:
Scenario Expected Actual result declared_file_type differs from the real file type failed with an input error code (ERR-AI-001) [fill in] limits.max_pages below the page count failed, ERR-UPL-004 [fill in] Body is not valid JSON Not processed; moved to the DLQ after 3 receives [fill in] The same analysis_requested sent twice (SQS redelivery) The worker reuses the runtime for the job_id, overwrites the result, never runs two copies in parallel [fill in] Worker stopped mid-job (docker compose stop worker, then start) The message reappears after the visibility timeout and the job resumes from the cache [fill in] Automated tests The repository ships an offline unit test suite (AWS mocked with Moto, fake model, real LangGraph):

title: Install and configure
content:
Run these on EC2 (Session Manager, user ubuntu), except step 3 which runs in CloudShell.
Install Docker Engine + the Compose plugin from Docker’s official repository, Git, Python 3.12 and the AWS CLI: sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl git python3.12-venv sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings sudo curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc] \ https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_CODENAME") stable" \ | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin sudo snap install aws-cli --classic sudo usermod -aG docker ubuntu exit # exit, then run "sudo su - ubuntu" again to pick up the docker group Check the tools and clone the repository into /opt (the data pipeline runs with ProtectHome=true, so it cannot read a checkout under /home). For a private repo, enter your username and a Personal Access Token when Git asks; never put the token in the URL. docker version && docker compose version && python3.12 --version && aws sts get-caller-identity sudo install -d -m 755 -o ubuntu -g ubuntu /opt/contract-risk-management git clone https://github.com/<ORG>/contract-risk-management.git /opt/contract-risk-management cd /opt/contract-risk-management && git rev-parse --short HEAD 📸 Screenshot to take: The Session Manager terminal after docker version && docker compose version && aws sts get-caller-identity: Compose ≥ 2.24 and an Arn containing assumed-role/ContractRisk-EC2-Role.

title: Proposal
content:
ContractGuard – AI Contract Risk Analysis on AWS A web app takes the contract; three AI agents read every clause, score risk against Vietnamese law and propose rewrites 1. Problem and solution overview Context
Small and medium businesses sign many service, purchase and outsourcing contracts, but rarely have a legal team to read every clause. The risk sits in penalties, liability caps, data protection, termination and governing law, and usually only shows up once a dispute starts. Having a lawyer review each contract is slow and expensive.
Target users
Group Need Procurement, sales and accounting staff in SMEs Know quickly which clauses are unfavourable before signing Small legal teams or in-house counsel Pre-screen contracts and focus on high-risk clauses Managers See risk scores across 7 domains and the organisation’s analysis history Solution
ContractGuard has two parts running in two AWS accounts:
Web application (application account): React served from Amazon S3 + CloudFront, an ASP.NET Core API on Amazon ECS Fargate, Google sign-in, business data in Supabase. Users upload a contract (PDF, DOCX, photo) to S3 with a signed URL, read the results, ask a chatbot about the contract and can cancel a running analysis. AI system (AI account): receives jobs through Amazon SQS and runs on Amazon EC2 in a private subnet, with three agents orchestrated by LangGraph: Agent Responsibility Agent 1 – Classification Splits the contract into clauses, assigns categories, extracts facts (parties, value, effective date…), keeping verbatim text and page numbers Agent 2 – Risk scoring Checks clauses against risk rules R01–R20 and 20 checks; looks up Vietnamese legal grounds through RAG Agent 3 – Recommendation Writes a mitigation and a rewritten clause for every finding, with sources; answers the chatbot The legal corpus is collected automatically from vanban.chinhphu.vn on an Amazon EventBridge schedule. Risk scores are computed by versioned code; the model never produces the number.
2. Problem statement Problem How the system solves it Manual review is slow and depends on legal expertise Three specialised agents work automatically; users read results with citations Language models can invent quotes or legal grounds Code checks that every quote is a verbatim substring of its clause; wrong findings are dropped and never scored The legal basis changes (new laws, amendments, repeals) The data pipeline keeps versions per Article with validity dates; RAG returns only provisions in force by default Contracts are in Vietnamese, English or both Bilingual prompts; explanations follow the user’s language, quotes keep their original language An analysis takes minutes; the web app cannot wait Asynchronous processing through SQS; the web app receives progress and results on a results queue Contracts are sensitive data The AI worker sits in a private subnet with no direct Internet route; telemetry carries no contract content; IAM permissions follow each role 3. Goals and scope Goals and outputs
Users sign in, upload a contract, follow progress (reading file → splitting clauses → evaluating → scoring) and get the result: clauses, findings with citations, scores for 7 risk domains, recommendations and rewritten clauses. A chatbot answers questions about an analysed contract, using only that contract’s clauses. Users can cancel a running analysis; a failed job is reported as failed with an error code instead of hanging. The legal corpus updates on a schedule (incremental daily, full weekly) and can be queried by validity date. Central monitoring: API logs in CloudWatch Logs, a trace per AI stage in Langfuse, alerts on failed jobs. Success criteria
Criterion How it is measured A test contract completes the path web → SQS → AI → S3 → result shown on the web E2E scenario; check extraction.json, DynamoDB completed, the completed message 100% of results match the extraction.v2 schema; 0 quotes outside their clause The backend checks schema and quotes before saving; unit tests No hanging jobs: every job ends as completed, failed or cancelled DynamoDB outcome table, Langfuse Cancelling stops the job within seconds Measured in a test scenario (local test: about 1 second) AWS cost stays within the FCAJ credit (about $200 per account) AWS Budgets, Pricing Calculator (section 6) All unit tests pass 281 tests on the AI side at the time of writing Scope
In scope Out of scope Web app (SPA + API), secure upload, chatbot, cancelling an analysis Digital signatures, contract lifecycle management, accounting integrations AI system: PDF/DOCX/OCR preprocessing, 3 agents, legal RAG, data pipeline Binding legal advice; results are for reference only A demo environment on AWS around the showcase; daily staging on Railway Multi-region production, SLAs, high availability for the AI worker Fit with Cloud and AWS
The system relies on AWS managed and serverless services: CloudFront, S3, ECS Fargate, SQS, DynamoDB on-demand, EventBridge Scheduler, Secrets Manager, Systems Manager, VPC Endpoints and IAM. The two accounts exchange data only through S3 and SQS with cross-account IAM; there is no direct network path between them.
4. Solution architecture Drawn in draw.io with the AWS Architecture Icons. Source file: docs/architecture/ContractGuard-Architecture.drawio in the AI project repository.
Flows (numbers on the diagram)
# Flow 1 Users open the app through Amazon CloudFront; the web frontend is served from Amazon S3 2 API calls go through CloudFront to the internal Application Load Balancer in the VPC, then to the API on ECS Fargate 3 Contracts are uploaded straight to Amazon S3 with a signed URL, without passing through the server 4 The API sends analysis requests, chat questions and cancel commands to Amazon SQS 5 The AI worker on EC2 takes jobs from SQS, records status in DynamoDB, sends the file to document processing, then passes the content to the 3 agents 6 LangGraph orchestrates the 3 agents; they call a language model (currently Google Gemini) and look up legal sources through MCP (Qdrant, Supabase, Tavily) 7 The worker writes the result to S3 and reports through SQS; the API validates it, stores it in Supabase and shows it to the user 8 EventBridge sends scheduled law-update commands to SQS; the data pipeline collects texts from vanban.chinhphu.vn, keeps the originals on S3 and updates the legal knowledge base 9 The worker’s private subnet has no route to the Internet: AWS services go through VPC Endpoints, everything else through the egress proxy (hostname allowlist) 10 A user cancels an analysis: the API sends a command on the cancel queue, the worker stops the job and moves on to the next contract 11 Administrators reach the AI EC2 only through AWS Systems Manager Session Manager: no SSH, no inbound port, no public IP AWS services and why they were chosen
Service Role Why Amazon CloudFront Single entry point: serves the SPA and forwards /api/* to the ALB Built-in HTTPS, static caching, keeps the ALB off the Internet (VPC origin); 1 TB/month free tier Amazon S3 (web) Stores the React build, read through Origin Access Control Cheap, 11 nines of durability, no server for the frontend Application Load Balancer Internal load balancer in an isolated subnet, reachable only from CloudFront Health checks, API kept off the Internet; ready for several tasks Amazon ECS Fargate (ARM64) Runs the ASP.NET Core API (0.5 vCPU, 1 GB) Serverless containers, no servers to manage; ARM is cheaper than x86; scale by configuration Amazon VPC (2 AZs, web) Network for the ALB and Fargate, no NAT Gateway No NAT keeps fixed cost low; the security group only lets the ALB reach the task Amazon CloudWatch Logs API logs, kept 2 weeks Native with ECS; short retention controls cost Amazon SES Email (member invitations, notifications) Managed, pay per email Amazon S3 (contracts) quarantine/ (uploads), clean/ (checked files), results/ (job requests and results) The two accounts exchange data by prefix; IAM permissions split by prefix Amazon SQS Analysis, results, chat, cancel and law-update queues; DLQ after 3 receives Decouples web and AI, survives worker restarts, redelivers messages when a worker dies mid-job Amazon EC2 (AI worker) Runs 9 Docker Compose containers and 2 systemd services The CPU embedding and rerank models need plenty of RAM (about 3.5 GB) and disk for the models; one machine mirrors the dev environment Amazon EC2 (egress proxy) Squid in a public subnet on a t3.micro Controls outbound Internet traffic with a hostname allowlist, cheaper than a NAT Gateway Amazon EBS gp3 Disks of both instances: images, models, SQLite volumes gp3 is cheaper than gp2, IOPS set separately VPC Endpoints Gateway (S3, DynamoDB) and interface (SQS, Secrets Manager, SSM, STS) The worker reaches AWS without an Internet route; gateway endpoints are free Amazon DynamoDB (on-demand) contract-risk-jobs (where each contract is now), contract-risk-job-events (each job’s outcome) Pay per request; conditional writes stop overwrites when a message is delivered twice Amazon EventBridge Scheduler Law collection schedule Serverless, no machine running cron AWS Secrets Manager Internal tokens and external API keys (Qdrant, Supabase, Tavily, Langfuse); the web’s database connection and Google OAuth No hard-coded credentials; each service gets only its own keys AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to administer EC2 No SSH, no bastion; audited through CloudTrail AWS IAM EC2 instance role, Fargate task role, GitHub OIDC deploy role No static access keys; least privilege by bucket/prefix, queue and table Services outside AWS
Service Role Why Google sign-in User sign-in No new password for users Supabase (PostgreSQL + pgvector) Web business data; legal tables of the data pipeline Free plan, does not use AWS credit Google Gemini API (gemini-3.5-flash-lite) Model of the 3 agents, with function calling Low token price, about 1M-token context Qdrant Cloud Legal vectors (dense 1024-d + sparse) Built-in hybrid search, free plan Tavily Web search when the legal corpus lacks evidence 1,000 free credits per month Langfuse Cloud Traces, tokens and errors of each AI stage Free Hobby plan AI system design (9 containers on the backend network + 2 systemd services)
Component Responsibility worker Takes SQS jobs, holds a DynamoDB lease, downloads from S3, writes results, deletes the message last; chat and cancel input-processing File checks, PDF/DOCX text, Vietnamese Tesseract OCR, chunks with source positions langgraph Agent 1 per chunk → aggregate → Agent 2 → Agent 3; cache/resume, scoring, builds the result agent-1, agent-2, agent-3 Three agents, each with its own prompts, model and memory mcp Read-only tool gateway for Agents 2/3: legal RAG, Qdrant, Supabase, S3, Tavily monitoring, config Sends traces to Langfuse; gives each service its secrets by token and allowlist contract-data-collector, contract-data-processor Collect laws, OCR, split Articles, write Supabase + Qdrant AWS Well-Architected Framework
Pillar Applied Gaps and next steps Security No static access keys: EC2 instance role, ECS task role, GitHub OIDC. Secrets in Secrets Manager, .env git-ignored, GitHub Push Protection. Worker in a private subnet, no public IP, no inbound Security Group rule, AWS APIs through VPC Endpoints, Internet through an allowlist proxy. ALB only reachable from CloudFront, web bucket behind OAC. Administration through Session Manager. The worker is denied writes to quarantine/ (roles kept apart). Containers run non-root with a read-only filesystem and no capabilities The AI containers share one instance role: block IMDS for containers that do not need AWS or split roles. SGs, routes, encryption at rest, CloudTrail and VPC Flow Logs still need verification Reliability SQS decouples web and AI, DLQ after 3 receives; DynamoDB lease and sequence prevent overwrites; idempotency keys; backoff retries for transient model errors; cache to resume after a crash; the message is deleted only after the result is stored; web VPC in 2 AZs One worker and one proxy, one AZ: if a machine fails, jobs wait in the queue until it is back. Next step: an Auto Scaling group or ECS driven by queue depth Operational Excellence Web infrastructure in AWS CDK (C#); GitHub Actions deploys; scripts start/stop the demo environment; JSON logs; Langfuse traces per job; a Langfuse check after deploy; a test runbook Add CloudWatch Alarms on the age of the oldest SQS message and a non-empty DLQ; AI logs are not yet in CloudWatch Performance Efficiency Fargate ARM64; asynchronous processing; embedding/rerank models preloaded and offline; hybrid search + rerank Qdrant Cloud runs in us-west-1; moving it to Singapore would cut latency Cost Optimization No NAT Gateway; free gateway endpoints; DynamoDB on-demand; free plans for Supabase/Qdrant/Tavily/Langfuse; AWS only up around the showcase, daily staging on Railway; logs kept 2 weeks Details in section 6 Sustainability Machines run only while there are users (the start/stop script includes both AI instances); ARM64 for the API — 5. Plan and timeline Adjust the weeks to match your actual worklog.
Week Work Milestone 1–2 Learn AWS basics (IAM, VPC, EC2, S3, SQS, DynamoDB); read the ContractGuard spec and design Requirements and the web–AI protocol understood 3–4 Architecture design, 3-agent and LangGraph skeleton, PDF/DOCX/OCR preprocessing 3-agent flow runs with a fake model 5–6 SQS/S3/DynamoDB worker, 9 containers packaged Local E2E with emulated AWS 7–8 MCP gateway, legal data pipeline, Qdrant, Supabase, hybrid RAG + rerank Legal lookup returns the right Article 9–10 Result schema, prompts for the 3 agents, scoring, web queues, chatbot Real job through the web’s queues 11 Langfuse monitoring, job cancel, DynamoDB status; private-subnet VPC, egress proxy, VPC Endpoints, Session Manager; EC2 deployment AI stack runs on EC2 in the isolated VPC 12 E2E tests with the web, AWS demo environment around the showcase, cost measurement, report Demo and report 6. Budget and cost estimation 6.1 Actual cost summary
Source: the “OJT” estimate created with AWS Pricing Calculator on 26 November 2026 from the AI account’s real usage in November 2026 (up to the 26th). Prices before discounts, in USD.
Item Usage Derived unit price Cost (USD) Share EC2 m7i-flex.large (AI worker) 58.8 hours $0.1197/hour 7.04 53.2% EBS gp3 61.2 GB-months $0.096/GB-month 5.88 44.5% Secrets Manager 0.38 secret-months, 268 calls $0.40/secret-month 0.15 1.1% EC2 data transfer 10.1 GB — 0.07 0.5% EC2 t3.micro (egress proxy) 4.2 hours $0.0132/hour 0.06 0.5% DynamoDB on-demand 12,590 WRU, 12,730 RRU — 0.01 0.1% Systems Manager 5 automation steps — 0.01 0.1% S3 0.05 GB-months, 799 requests — 0.003 < 0.1% Total (before discounts) 13.22 100% Actually billed 0.05 The rest was covered by Free Tier/credits Findings from the real data
Compute (EC2) and disk (EBS) make up 97.7%. The serverless services (SQS, DynamoDB, S3, Secrets Manager) together stay under 1.5%. EBS is billed by size even while the instance is stopped: 61.2 GB-months over 26 days is about 70 GB of disk. There is no line yet for interface endpoints (SQS, Secrets Manager, SSM, STS) or the proxy’s public IPv4. Both are billed per hour and must be added to the estimate. Some traffic goes to us-west-1: Qdrant Cloud runs in the US. 6.2 Monthly estimate
Assumptions:
Demo month: the AI worker and proxy run 8 hours/day × 22 days = 176 hours. The web runs on AWS only for 3 days around the showcase; daily staging runs on Railway (outside AWS). 24/7: 730 hours for both accounts. Load: 100 analyses and 500 chat questions per month. Each analysis is about 100k input and 30k output tokens; each chat question 10k input and 2k output (system design estimate, to be measured with Langfuse). EC2, EBS and Secrets Manager unit prices come from the “OJT” estimate. Public IPv4 is $0.005/hour (VPC pricing page). The web side uses the web team’s design estimate (ALB about $18 and a 0.25 vCPU Fargate task about $8 when running 24/7), with Fargate doubled for the current 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB task. Gemini gemini-3.5-flash-lite paid tier: $0.30 per 1M input tokens, $2.50 per 1M output tokens. Item Demo month (USD) 24/7 (USD) Calculation EC2 m7i-flex.large (AI worker) 21.07 87.38 hours × $0.1197 EC2 t3.micro (proxy) 2.32 9.64 hours × $0.0132 Proxy public IPv4 0.88 3.65 hours × $0.005 EBS gp3 70 GB 6.72 6.72 70 × $0.096, billed while stopped too Secrets Manager, DynamoDB, SQS, S3, SSM 0.60 0.70 from real usage, mostly within the free tier AI account 31.59 108.09 ALB 1.78 18.00 72 hours / 730 hours ECS Fargate ARM64 (0.5 vCPU, 1 GB) 1.58 16.00 Fargate task public IPv4 0.36 3.65 CloudFront, S3, CloudWatch Logs, SES, Secrets Manager 1.00 5.00 CloudFront and SQS within the free tier Web account 4.72 42.65 Gemini API 14.50 14.50 100 × $0.105 + 500 × $0.008 Supabase, Qdrant, Tavily, Langfuse 0 0 free plans Total ≈ 50.8 ≈ 165.2 Interface endpoints are not included: AWS bills each endpoint per hour in each AZ, even while the instances are stopped. With 4–5 endpoints in one AZ this could be about $30–50/month if left on all month, the largest item after EC2. Check it with Pricing Calculator.
Quick statistics
Metric Value Cost of one analysis (Gemini) about $0.105 Cost of one chat question (Gemini) about $0.008 Demo month: AWS / model $36.3 (71%) / $14.5 (29%) Saving from running only during demo hours vs 24/7 about 69% (≈ $114/month) FCAJ credit per account (about $200) lasts about 6 demo months on the AI account; about 1.8 months at 24/7 6.3 Cost optimization
Run only when used: a script starts/stops the demo environment together with both AI instances; the web runs on AWS only around the showcase and is developed daily on Railway. Egress proxy and free gateway endpoints: use a t3.micro egress proxy for outbound traffic; S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints are free. Create only the interface endpoints that are needed, and delete them during long shutdowns. Right-size machines and disks: shrink EBS to real usage, delete volumes and snapshots not attached to any instance; consider Savings Plans for long-term use. Serverless, pay per use: SQS, DynamoDB on-demand, EventBridge Scheduler, Fargate ARM64. Data lifecycle: S3 Lifecycle for results/ and quarantine/; CloudWatch Logs kept 2 weeks. Model cost: track tokens in Langfuse; use the Gemini Batch API for bulk evaluation runs (about 50% cheaper). Budget alerts: AWS Budgets at 50% and 80% of the credit, email to the whole team. 7. Risks and mitigation Risk matrix
Gemini rate limits (429) or 5xx errors: High impact, medium likelihood. Model output breaks the schema or invents quotes: High impact, medium likelihood. Prompt injection inside the contract: High impact, low likelihood. The worker dies mid-job, SQS delivers twice: Medium impact, medium likelihood. The AI instance or the proxy fails: High impact, low likelihood. Credential leak: High impact, low likelihood. AI containers share one instance role: Medium impact, medium likelihood. Credit runs out or a machine is left running: High impact, medium likelihood. Supabase Free pauses after a week of inactivity: Medium impact, medium likelihood. Two APIs (AWS and Railway) read the results queue: Medium impact, medium likelihood. Outdated legal corpus: Medium impact, medium likelihood. Mitigation strategy
Gemini API errors: Client retries 5 times following retryDelay; LangGraph retries a node 3 times (backoff 5→60 s) only for transient errors. Hallucinations and invalid schema: Schema check with up to 2 repair requests; wrong quotes are dropped and not scored; the backend validates again before saving. Prompt injection: Treat the contract strictly as data in the prompt; keep MCP tools read-only and scope source document access to its own job. Worker crash and duplicate SQS delivery: DynamoDB lease, idempotency keys, and cache to resume; delete the SQS message only after storing the result; route failures to DLQ after 3 receives. Instance or proxy failure: Containers restart automatically; later scale with an Auto Scaling group or ECS driven by queue depth. Credential security: No static access keys; store secrets in Secrets Manager, use GitHub OIDC and Push Protection; block IMDS for containers that do not need AWS or split roles per workload. Cost overrun: AWS Budgets alerts at 50%/80% of credit, start/stop scripts for the demo environment, and monitoring interface endpoints and EBS volumes. Supabase Free inactivity: Resume the project before the demo, or upgrade to Pro ($25/month) for long-term use. Queue contention (AWS vs. Railway): Stop the Railway API while the AWS environment is active (runbook procedure). Legal corpus freshness: Run incremental daily and full weekly collection with version and validity tracking per Article. Contingency plan
If the AI instance or proxy goes down, jobs remain safely in SQS until the machine is back and resume from cached intermediate state. If a job fails unrecoverably, report failed with an error code and move the message to the DLQ instead of hanging. If AWS credits run low or the demo environment is shut down, keep daily staging running on Railway. Use AWS CDK (C#) and GitHub Actions to redeploy or restore the web infrastructure consistently if needed. 8. Expected results A product running on AWS: users upload a contract, get results with citations, scores and recommendations, and ask the chatbot. A versioned, self-updating Vietnamese legal corpus usable for RAG. A Well-Architected design: no hard-coded credentials, no direct Internet route for the worker, fault-tolerant asynchronous processing, cost controlled with real data. A base to grow: more contract types, a different model, the worker on ECS or an Auto Scaling group when needed.

title: Create DynamoDB tables
content:
contract-risk-jobs holds the current state of each contract (key contract:<contract_id>): runtime, lease, stage, progress. contract-risk-job-events holds the append-only history. content:

Monitoring strips contract content and secrets, stores them in SQLite, then exports OTLP to Langfuse Cloud when LANGFUSE_ENABLED=true and the keys are in Secrets Manager (step 5.4.4). title: Store API keys in Secrets Manager
content:
The config service reads this JSON secret at start-up and gives each service only the keys it is allowed (config/policy.json): for example only mcp receives the Qdrant/Supabase/Tavily keys and only monitoring receives the Langfuse keys. The commands read keys with read -s (not echoed, not stored in shell history) and generate the two internal tokens randomly.
source ~/cr.env read -rsp "Tavily API key: " TAVILY && echo read -rp "Qdrant URL: " QDRANT_URL read -rsp "Qdrant API key: " QDRANT_KEY && echo read -rp "Supabase Project URL: " SUPABASE_URL read -rsp "Supabase publishable key: " SUPABASE_PUB && echo read -rsp "Supabase secret key: " SUPABASE_SECRET && echo read -rsp "Langfuse public key: " LF_PUBLIC && echo read -rsp "Langfuse secret key: " LF_SECRET && echo umask 077 jq -n --arg internal "$(openssl rand -hex 32)" --arg mcp "$(openssl rand -hex 32)" \ --arg tavily "$TAVILY" --arg qurl "$QDRANT_URL" --arg qkey "$QDRANT_KEY" \ --arg surl "$SUPABASE_URL" --arg spub "$SUPABASE_PUB" --arg ssec "$SUPABASE_SECRET" \ --arg lpub "$LF_PUBLIC" --arg lsec "$LF_SECRET" \ '{INTERNAL_API_TOKEN:$internal, MCP_API_TOKEN:$mcp, TAVILY_API_KEY:$tavily, QDRANT_URL:$qurl, QDRANT_API_KEY:$qkey, SUPABASE_URL:$surl, SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY:$spub, SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY:$ssec, LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY:$lpub, LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY:$lsec}' > /tmp/api-keys.json aws secretsmanager create-secret --name contract-risk/prod/api-keys \ --description "ContractGuard AI service keys" --secret-string file:///tmp/api-keys.json shred -u /tmp/api-keys.json unset TAVILY QDRANT_KEY SUPABASE_PUB SUPABASE_SECRET LF_PUBLIC LF_SECRET The Gemini key is not in this secret: the code only reads GEMINI_API_KEY from the .env file on EC2 (step 5.5.2). title: Workshop
content:
Deploying a multi-agent AI contract risk analysis system on AWS Overview This workshop deploys ContractGuard AI from scratch in one AWS account: build a secure VPC, create a least-privilege IAM role, create SQS queues, S3 buckets, DynamoDB tables and a Secrets Manager secret, then run 9 Docker containers and the legal data pipeline on Amazon EC2. You will practise:
Network and security: VPC, subnet, a Security Group with no inbound port, VPC Gateway Endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, an IAM instance role with IMDSv2. Secret management: API keys live in Secrets Manager and the host’s .env, never hard-coded in code or GitHub. Monitoring: per-stage traces and tokens on Langfuse, metrics/alerts from the monitoring service. title: Legal data pipeline
content:
The legal corpus used by RAG is loaded by two systemd services running outside Docker on the same EC2 host:
collector: takes a message from the contract-risk-data-update SQS queue, downloads documents from vanban.chinhphu.vn, stores the originals in the reference S3 bucket and hands the bytes in memory to the processor; processor: text extraction/OCR, splitting per Article, validity and amendment relations, writes Supabase and dense + sparse vectors to Qdrant; retries failed jobs periodically. Create the schema in Supabase: open the project → SQL Editor, run data_pipeline/migrations/001_legal_schema.sql, then 002_versions_without_s3_json.sql. 📸 Screenshot to take: Supabase → SQL Editor after running 001_legal_schema.sql (Success), and the Table Editor listing legal_documents, legal_document_versions, legal_articles, legal_relations, ingest_jobs, crawl_runs.
Install and try one document (--limit 1 really writes to S3/Supabase/Qdrant), then start both services: cd /opt/contract-risk-management sudo sh infrastructure/ec2/data_pipeline_setup.sh sudo -u contract-data test -r .env && sudo -u contract-data test -r models && echo "readable" sudo systemctl stop contract-data-collector sudo -u contract-data env PYTHONPATH="$PWD" \ /opt/contract-risk/data-pipeline/.venv/bin/python -m data_pipeline collect --mode incremental --limit 1 sudo systemctl start contract-data-processor contract-data-collector sudo systemctl status contract-data-collector contract-data-processor --no-pager 📸 Screenshot to take: The systemctl status output of contract-data-collector and contract-data-processor: active (running).
Trigger one collection run through SQS (from CloudShell). One message is one run; use full to sweep the whole list: source ~/cr.env aws sqs send-message --queue-url "$DATA_URL" --message-body '{"mode":"incremental"}' Follow the logs on EC2: sudo journalctl -u contract-data-collector -u contract-data-processor -n 100 --no-pager 📸 Screenshot to take: journalctl after sending {"mode":"incremental"}: run_id, number of documents processed, no error.
📸 Screenshot to take: Two images combined: the Supabase Table Editor showing rows in legal_articles; the Qdrant Cloud legal_documents collection with Points count > 0; optionally aws s3 ls s3://<LEGAL_BUCKET>/legal/ --recursive | head.
To automate it, a schedule (for example EventBridge Scheduler) can send {"mode":"incremental"} daily and {"mode":"full"} weekly to this queue. The first run can take a while because embeddings are computed on CPU.

title: Troubleshooting and lessons learned
content: Issues met and how they were solved Issue Cause Fix Containers report NoCredentialsError while aws works on the host IMDS hop limit = 1 blocks requests coming through the bridge network Set HttpPutResponseHopLimit=2; preflight.sh checks STS from inside a container GitHub Push Protection rejected the push The Gemini key was hard-coded in common/settings.py Removed the key from code, read only GEMINI_API_KEY from .env (gitignored), rewrote the unpushed commit, rotated the key Gemini returns 400 on the second tool round Gemini 3 requires each functionCall’s thoughtSignature to be sent back The client keeps the signature in the tool call and the agent puts it back in the transcript MALFORMED_FUNCTION_CALL The prompt told the model to call a tool on a turn with no tools offered Only ask for tools when the agent has them (Agents 2/3) DynamoDB progress went backwards from agent_3 to agent_1 The reflect span (long-term memory) after Agent 3 counted as a stage Monitoring ignores reflect spans when computing progress 429 even for short answers The provider counts max_output_tokens against the tokens-per-minute limit as soon as the request arrives Size max_completion_tokens per agent (32k/64k/32k) systemd could not read the source ProtectHome=true hides /home Clone into /opt/contract-risk-management An LLM agent could read the web app’s business tables through Supabase App tables shared the public schema and the secret key bypasses RLS App tables moved to the app schema; MCP only exposes the tables in SUPABASE_TABLES Changing the embedding model broke search Vector size differed from the old Qdrant collection Recreated a 1024-d + sparse collection and re-indexed; documented “new tokenizer = re-index” Lessons learned Check permissions from inside the container, not just on the host. Never write a secret into code, even “just for a test”; enable secret scanning from day one. LLM output is untrusted data: always verify it in code (schema, verbatim quotes, code-computed scores). Delete the SQS message only as the very last step, after the result is durably stored. Future work Move the worker to Amazon ECS and scale on queue depth. Put EC2 in a private subnet with Interface Endpoints and a NAT Gateway when the budget allows. Infrastructure as code (AWS CDK or Terraform) and CI/CD with GitHub Actions using OIDC. A quality evaluation set (finding recall/precision) on labelled contracts.

content:
Congratulations on finishing the workshop! Delete every resource in reverse order so no cost keeps accruing.
On EC2 (Session Manager), stop the data pipeline and the Docker stack: cd /opt/contract-risk-management sudo systemctl disable --now contract-data-collector contract-data-processor docker compose down In CloudShell, delete the AWS resources: source ~/cr.env # 1. EC2 aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" aws ec2 wait instance-terminated --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" # 2. Network for EP in $(aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints --filters Name=vpc-id,Values="$VPC_ID" \ --query 'VpcEndpoints[].VpcEndpointId' --output text); do aws ec2 delete-vpc-endpoints --vpc-endpoint-ids "$EP" done aws ec2 delete-security-group --group-id "$SG_ID" aws ec2 delete-subnet --subnet-id "$SUBNET_ID" aws ec2 delete-route-table --route-table-id "$RT_ID" aws ec2 detach-internet-gateway --internet-gateway-id "$IGW_ID" --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" aws ec2 delete-internet-gateway --internet-gateway-id "$IGW_ID" aws ec2 delete-vpc --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" # 3. S3 (empty, then delete) for B in "$DOCS_BUCKET" "$LEGAL_BUCKET"; do aws s3 rb "s3://$B" --force; done # 4. SQS (main queues and DLQs) for Q in analysis-requests analysis-results chat-requests data-update; do for N in "contract-risk-$Q" "contract-risk-$Q-dlq"; do aws sqs delete-queue --queue-url "$(aws sqs get-queue-url --queue-name "$N" --query QueueUrl --output text)" done done # 5. DynamoDB aws dynamodb delete-table --table-name contract-risk-jobs aws dynamodb delete-table --table-name contract-risk-job-events # 6. Secrets Manager (immediate, no recovery window) aws secretsmanager delete-secret --secret-id contract-risk/prod/api-keys --force-delete-without-recovery # 7. IAM aws iam remove-role-from-instance-profile --instance-profile-name ContractRisk-EC2-Profile --role-name ContractRisk-EC2-Role aws iam delete-instance-profile --instance-profile-name ContractRisk-EC2-Profile aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name ContractRisk-EC2-Role --policy-name contract-risk-runtime aws iam detach-role-policy --role-name ContractRisk-EC2-Role --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore aws iam delete-role --role-name ContractRisk-EC2-Role rm -f ~/cr.env request.json req-*.json extraction.json aws s3 rb --force and --force-delete-without-recovery delete permanently and cannot be undone. Double-check the bucket and secret names before running them.
External services: delete the lab’s Qdrant cluster and Supabase project (if you no longer need them), revoke the Gemini key in Google AI Studio, the Tavily key and the Langfuse keys. Delete the AWS Budgets budget if you no longer need it. 📸 Screenshot to take: Combined image: EC2 Terminated, the VPC list without contract-risk-vpc, no contract-risk-* resources left in S3/SQS/DynamoDB.
📸 Screenshot to take: Billing → Cost Explorer (or Bills) one day after clean-up: no service cost still growing.
